# Retry policies are a gateway capability, not a client detail

Most services hardcode one retry rule inside every client. When the rule has to change, every caller changes with it, and nobody can say which routes retry what.

## The problem

A checkout call, a nightly export and a payment write all fail differently. The checkout call needs a fast retry with jitter. The export can wait and try again every minute. The payment write must never be retried blindly, because a duplicate charge costs more than a failed request.

When the rule lives inside each client, three things go wrong. The rules drift apart as teams copy and tweak them. Tests need real clocks and real sleeps. And a change of policy becomes a change of code in many repositories.

## What you get

- One place that decides how a route retries.
- Policies you can test in microseconds with a fake clock.
- A different rule for each call site, without a chain of conditionals.

## The design

The client asks a policy object for the next delay and for whether it may try again. The policy is chosen per route by the gateway, so the client never learns which rule it follows.

```java
public interface RetryPolicy {
    Optional<Duration> nextDelay(int attempt, Throwable failure);
}

public final class ExponentialBackoff implements RetryPolicy {
    public Optional<Duration> nextDelay(int attempt, Throwable failure) {
        if (attempt >= 5) {
            return Optional.empty();
        }
        long millis = 100L << attempt;
        return Optional.of(Duration.ofMillis(millis));
    }
}
```

A fixed delay and a never-retry policy implement the same interface in a few lines each. The repository holds all three, the class diagram and the tests.

![Class diagram](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/example-owner/retry-policies/0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567/docs/diagrams/class.png)

## The architecture view

Seen from the system, the same idea is a resilience policy table at the gateway: one row per route, one policy per row. Changing a row changes behaviour for every client behind that route, and the table is the single document a reviewer has to read.

![Gateway policy table](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/example-owner/retry-policies/0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567/docs/diagrams/gateway.png)

## Field notes

A retry rule that nobody owns tends to grow a new special case every quarter. Exponential backoff without jitter makes every waiting client wake up at the same instant. A policy object makes the decision visible, and a visible decision can be reviewed. A policy table is easier to audit than retry code scattered across a dozen repositories. Circuit breakers and retries interact, so decide which one sits outside the other on purpose.

Tests with a fake clock finish in microseconds and never flake on a slow build agent. Metrics per policy show which rule is working and which one only adds load. A retry budget caps the extra load a failing dependency can receive from all callers together. Start with the routes that page you at night, and leave the quiet ones alone. Do not let the client inspect the policy; it should only ask for the next delay.

Timeouts belong in the same table, because a retry without a deadline is just a slow failure. Changing a row in the table should need a review, but never a release of the clients. Fallbacks are a separate decision and deserve their own place in the same table. Dry-run a new policy against recorded traffic before it touches a live route. A shared vocabulary of policy names makes conversations between teams much shorter.

A failing dependency should see less traffic over time, never more. Treat a change of policy like a change of schema: small, reversible and announced. The best policy for a route is often the one that gives up early and says why. A retry rule that nobody owns tends to grow a new special case every quarter. Exponential backoff without jitter makes every waiting client wake up at the same instant.

When two routes need the same rule, name it once and reference it twice. Teams copy the client library, change one constant, and forget to tell anyone. A fixed delay is a fine default for batch jobs, because nobody is waiting on the result. Tests with a fake clock finish in microseconds and never flake on a slow build agent. Metrics per policy show which rule is working and which one only adds load.

Idempotency keys turn a dangerous retry into a safe one, but only when the server honours them. The gateway already knows the route, the caller and the method, so it is the natural place to choose a rule. Write the policy name into the log line, and the incident review becomes much shorter. Timeouts belong in the same table, because a retry without a deadline is just a slow failure. Changing a row in the table should need a review, but never a release of the clients.

Circuit breakers and retries interact, so decide which one sits outside the other on purpose. Document why each route has its rule, not only what the rule is. Keep the policy interface small, so a new rule is a few lines and a test. A failing dependency should see less traffic over time, never more. Treat a change of policy like a change of schema: small, reversible and announced.

Do not let the client inspect the policy; it should only ask for the next delay. Review the table together with the on-call team, because they feel the cost of a wrong row. Measure the effect of every change, and keep the old row until the numbers agree. When two routes need the same rule, name it once and reference it twice. ## Next steps

Open the repository, run the tests and swap the policy for one route. Then tell me which retry rule has bitten you in production.
